exercises.title: Break It, Then Fix It
exercises.brief: Write three small, valid HTML snippets of your choosing (a paragraph, a link, an image). For each one, deliberately introduce one mistake — an unclosed tag, an unquoted attribute, a misspelled tag name — and note in one sentence what you'd expect to visibly break versus what might silently misbehave instead.

quiz.question: What is the core relationship between a tag and an attribute in HTML?
options: They're interchangeable terms for the same thing.
Attributes define what the element is; tags are purely decorative.
Only some elements have tags, while all elements require attributes.
The tag defines what the element fundamentally is; attributes add configuration or detail without changing that core identity.
quiz.explanation: The tag name establishes the element's identity (a paragraph, a link, an image); attributes like href, class, or alt add detail on top of that identity without changing what kind of element it fundamentally is.

quiz.question:
A developer forgets to close a

tag before starting a new one. What's the most accurate description of what happens?
options: The page fails to load entirely, showing a blank screen.
The browser throws a visible error message the developer can't miss.
The browser silently closes the unclosed tag and continues, which can quietly change the document's actual nesting without any visible error.
Nothing happens — HTML doesn't require closing tags at all.
quiz.explanation: HTML parsers are built to recover from broken markup by guessing and continuing, rather than stopping outright. That means an unclosed tag often produces no visible error at all — just a silently different document structure than you intended, which is exactly why it's easy to miss.

summary: Elements are built from tags (which establish what an element fundamentally is) and attributes (which configure or describe it without changing that identity). Because browsers recover from broken markup by guessing rather than erroring out, unclosed tags and unquoted attributes rarely announce themselves — they just quietly produce a document structure different from the one you intended.
interviewQuestions: What's the difference between a tag and an attribute?
Why might invalid HTML render 'fine' visually but still be considered broken?

title: Headings, Paragraphs, and Text
description: Building a correct, skip-free heading outline that both sighted readers and screen readers rely on.
learningObjectives: Apply headings h1-h6 and paragraphs to produce a document with a correct, non-skipping outline.
Identify a heading hierarchy mistake (a skipped level) in a piece of markup.
Choose a heading level based on document outline logic, not desired font size.

sections.text: Quick Recap Before You Practice

Headings (h1–h6) and paragraphs create a readable document outline that both humans and screen readers rely on. h1 is the top-level heading (usually one per page), h2 is a subheading under it, h3 a subheading under that, and so on — the number is the outline level, not a font-size dial. Paragraphs (

) hold the actual prose underneath. That's genuinely the whole rule; the rest of this lesson is drilling it until choosing the right level is automatic.

sections.title: A correct outline
sections.code:
Recipe: Weeknight Hummus

A quick, no-fuss hummus you can make in ten minutes.

Ingredients

Chickpeas, tahini, lemon, garlic, olive oil.

Steps

1. Drain and rinse

Drain the chickpeas and rinse under cold water.

2. Blend

Combine everything and blend until smooth.

sections.text: Choosing heading levels by font size desired instead of document outline logic — skipping from h1 to h4 because it 'happened to look like the right size' — is the mistake to drill against here. It breaks the outline a screen reader announces to a blind user navigating heading-by-heading, and it confuses search engines about your page's actual structure. If you want smaller text, that's a CSS decision; the heading level is a structural decision, made separately.

sections.title: Drill: Fix the Skipped Heading Levels
sections.instructions: This page's heading outline skips from a top-level heading straight to a deeply nested one, with two levels missing in between. Fix the JSX so the heading levels step down one at a time (h1 → h2 → h3), without changing the visible text.

sections.label: Without a reference, write a 3-level heading outline (h1, then two h2s, then one h3 under one of them) for any topic of your choosing, with a paragraph under each heading.
sections.hint: Draw the outline as a bulleted list first if that helps — h1 at the top, h2s as its children, h3 as a child of one h2.

exercises.title: Escalating Drill: Outline Three Documents
exercises.brief: Write correct heading + paragraph markup for three short documents: (1) a recipe with an ingredients section and a steps section, (2) a product page with a description and a specs section, (3) a blog post with an introduction, two supporting sections, and a conclusion. Each must have exactly one h1 and a heading hierarchy that never skips a level.

quiz.question: A page uses <h1> for its title, then <h2> for two section headings, then jumps straight to <h4> for a sub-point under one section. What's wrong with this?
options: It skips h3, breaking the outline that screen readers and search engines rely on to understand document structure.
Nothing — heading levels are purely cosmetic and any order is fine.
You're only allowed to use h1 and h2 in valid HTML.
The page will fail to render because of the skipped level.
quiz.explanation: Heading levels represent nesting in a document outline, not visual styling choices. Skipping from h2 to h4 breaks that outline logic for anyone or anything relying on it — most notably screen reader users navigating heading-by-heading, and search engines parsing page structure.

quiz.question: A developer wants a subheading to appear smaller than their h1 but chooses <h3> specifically because 'it's the size I want,' skipping h2 entirely. What's the better approach?
options: This is correct — heading levels exist specifically to control size.

Avoid headings altogether and use styled

tags instead.
Use h2 for correct outline structure, and control the visual size separately with CSS.
Use h6 instead, since lower numbers are always more prominent.
quiz.explanation: Heading level should be chosen for outline correctness (what level of the document hierarchy this heading represents), not for a desired font size. If h2's default size doesn't look right, that's what CSS is for — the two concerns are meant to be handled separately.

summary: Headings (h1–h6) and paragraphs build a document's readable outline, one that both sighted readers skimming the page and screen reader users navigating by heading rely on. The level you choose should reflect where a heading sits in that outline — never the font size you want, which is a separate, CSS-only decision.
interviewQuestions: Why shouldn't you choose a heading level based on how big you want the text to look?
How does a skipped heading level affect a screen reader user, specifically?

title: Links, Images, and Paths
description: Connecting documents and media with and , and the difference between relative and absolute paths.
learningObjectives: Apply anchor and img elements to connect documents and media.
Explain the difference between a relative path and an absolute path, with an example of each.
Identify why a local absolute file path breaks once a site is deployed.

sections.text: Quick Recap Before You Practice

Anchor and img elements connect documents and media; relative vs absolute paths determine how the browser resolves them. links to another page or resource; embeds an image directly in the page. Both need a path telling the browser where to find the thing — and that path can be written two fundamentally different ways.

sections.title: Relative vs. absolute paths
sections.code: Read the post Read the post

sections.text: Using an absolute local file path that breaks once the site is deployed is this lesson's core trap. It's an easy mistake to miss, because it works flawlessly the entire time you're building locally — the file really is at that path on your machine. The instant the site is deployed to a server, that path points to a folder structure that doesn't exist there, and every one of those images or links quietly breaks at once.

sections.title: Drill: Fix the Broken Path Pattern
sections.instructions: This card links to a hardcoded local-style absolute path, which is exactly the pattern that breaks on deploy. Edit the JSX to use a relative-style path instead (e.g. "images/logo.png" instead of a full local path), and add descriptive alt text for the image — which is currently missing.

sections.text: Notice the alt attribute in that example was left empty. It's easy to treat alt as an afterthought, but it's read aloud by screen readers in place of the image, and it's what displays if the image fails to load — which, per the Network panel lesson back in module-0-2, happens more often than you'd think. A missing or empty alt on a meaningful image is a genuine accessibility failure, not a nitpick.

sections.label: Write a valid element for a photo of a red bicycle at the path "images/bike.jpg", with meaningful alt text — then explain in one sentence why the alt text you chose is better than something generic like "image."
sections.hint: Alt text should describe what the image conveys, as if you were describing it to someone who can't see it.

exercises.title: Escalating Drill: Links and Images
exercises.brief: Write markup for: (1) a link to an external site opening in a new tab, (2) a relative link to a page at /contact on the same site, (3) an image with a relative path and meaningful alt text, (4) an image wrapped in a link (so clicking the image navigates somewhere) — with the image's alt text written for its role as a link, not just as a picture.

quiz.question: A developer's images all display correctly while developing locally, using paths like "/Users/dana/site/images/logo.png". After deploying to a live server, none of the images load. What's the most likely cause?
options: The absolute local file paths pointed to a folder structure that only exists on the developer's own machine, and doesn't exist on the server.
The images were deleted during deployment.
img elements don't work on deployed websites.
The alt text was missing, which prevents images from loading.
quiz.explanation: An absolute local path like /Users/dana/... only resolves correctly on that specific machine. It works flawlessly during local development because the file really is there — but a deployed server has an entirely different file structure, so every image using that pattern breaks at once, all silently, with no error beyond a missing image.

quiz.question: Why does the alt attribute on an matter beyond just 'being good practice'?
options: It has no real functional purpose; it's purely a formality.
It only affects how fast the image loads.
It's required only for images larger than a certain file size.
It's read aloud by screen readers in place of the image, and displayed if the image fails to load.
quiz.explanation: alt text serves two concrete, functional purposes: it's what a screen reader announces instead of the image, and it's what displays as fallback text if the image request fails — which, as covered in the Network panel lesson, is a real and common occurrence, not a hypothetical.

summary: Anchor and img elements connect documents and media, and the path you give them can be absolute (a full address, works anywhere) or relative (resolved from the current page's location). Absolute local file paths are the trap: they work perfectly during local development and break silently, all at once, the moment a site is deployed. alt text isn't optional decoration — it's what a screen reader announces and what displays when an image request fails.
interviewQuestions: What's the difference between a relative and an absolute path, and when would you use each?
Why might all of a site's images work locally but break entirely after deployment?
What's the functional (not just 'best practice') purpose of an image's alt attribute?

title: Lists and Tables
description: Choosing between lists and tables to model sequence versus grid data — and why tables-for-layout hurts accessibility.
learningObjectives: Apply lists (ul/ol/li) and tables (table/tr/td/th) to model the correct kind of structured data.
Choose ordered vs. unordered lists correctly based on whether sequence matters.
Explain why using a table for page layout, instead of tabular data, harms accessibility.

sections.text: Quick Recap Before You Practice

Lists (ul/ol/li) and tables (table/tr/td/th) each model a specific kind of structured data — sequence vs grid. A list is for items where you group related things together; use <ol> (ordered) when their order carries meaning — like steps in a recipe — and <ul> (unordered) when it doesn't, like a set of tags. A table is for genuinely two-dimensional, grid-shaped data, where both rows and columns carry meaning — think a spreadsheet, not a page layout.

sections.text: Using a table for page layout instead of tabular data, hurting accessibility, was a genuinely common practice in the early web — dividing a whole page into invisible table cells to position a sidebar, header, and content column. A screen reader encountering that announces 'table, three columns, one row' before reading any actual content, which is confusing at best and actively misleading about what the page is. If you're not looking at a genuine grid of rows and meaningful columns, a table is the wrong tool — you'll get real, purpose-built layout tools starting in module-1-2.

sections.title: Drill: Ordered, Unordered, or Table?
sections.instructions: Three pieces of content below are marked up with the wrong structure: a sequence of numbered instructions using <ul> instead of <ol>, a set of unordered tags using <ol>, and genuinely tabular data crammed into a bulleted list. Fix all three to use the correct structure.

sections.label: Explain, without a reference, the specific test you'd use to decide between an <ol> and a <ul> for a given set of items — and separately, the test for whether something belongs in a <table> at all.
sections.hint: One test is about whether reordering the items would change their meaning. The other is about whether both rows AND columns carry meaning.

exercises.title: Escalating Drill: Choose the Right Structure
exercises.brief: Mark up three pieces of content with the correct structure: (1) a numbered set of driving directions, (2) an unordered list of a restaurant's dietary accommodation icons, (3) a small table comparing three phone models across price and storage — genuinely two-dimensional data, not a layout trick.

quiz.question: A set of navigation links (Home, About, Contact) is marked up as an <ol>. Is this the right choice?
options: Yes — navigation should always use ordered lists.
It doesn't matter — ol and ul are visually and semantically identical.
No — navigation links should never be in a list at all.
No — the order of these links carries no real meaning, so <ul> is the correct, more accurate choice.
quiz.explanation: The test for ol vs. ul is whether reordering the items would change their meaning. Reordering 'Home, About, Contact' doesn't change what the navigation means, so ul is the semantically correct choice — ol implies a meaningful sequence, like ranked results or numbered steps.

quiz.question: A developer uses a <table> to position a page's header, sidebar, and main content into three columns. What's the main problem with this?
options: Tables can't visually create multi-column layouts.
It's slower to render than any other approach.
A screen reader will announce this as tabular data ('table, three columns'), which is confusing and inaccurate since it's actually page layout, not a data grid.
There's no real problem — this is a standard, recommended technique.
quiz.explanation: Tables carry specific semantic meaning — rows and columns of related data. Using one purely to position layout regions makes a screen reader announce structure that doesn't reflect what's actually there, which is exactly the kind of meaning-appearance mismatch this whole module has been building intuition against.

summary: Lists model sequence-shaped or grouped data — <ol> when order carries meaning, <ul> when it doesn't — while tables model genuinely two-dimensional data, where both rows and columns matter. Using a table purely for page layout was a common early-web habit that actively harms accessibility, since it announces structure that doesn't match what the content actually is.
interviewQuestions: How do you decide between an ordered list and an unordered list?
Why is using tables for page layout considered bad practice today?

title: Forms and User Input
description: Collecting user input with inputs, labels, and a submit action — and why label association isn't optional.
learningObjectives: Implement: forms collect user input via inputs, labels, and a submit action.
Correctly associate a <label> with its <input> using for/id.
Predict which input type (text, email, checkbox, etc.) fits a given kind of data before checking.

sections.text: Every Sign-Up, Every Search Box, Every Checkout

Forms collect user input via inputs, labels, and a submit action; label association is essential for usability. Nearly every interaction where a user gives an app information — signing up, searching, checking out — runs through a <form> containing <input> elements. Get comfortable here, because you'll be writing forms constantly.

sections.title: A minimal, correctly labeled form
sections.code:
<form>
  <label for="email">Email address</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email">

  <label for="newsletter">Subscribe to updates</label>
  <input type="checkbox" id="newsletter" name="newsletter">

  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>

sections.text: That for/id pairing — the label's for matching the input's id — is doing more work than it looks like. It's what lets a sighted user click the label text itself (not just the tiny checkbox) to focus or toggle the input, and it's what a screen reader announces when the input receives focus. Without it, a visually adjacent label and input have zero actual relationship as far as the browser or assistive tech is concerned — they're just two elements that happen to be near each other.

Leaving out <label> or its 'for' attribute, making the field unusable for screen reader and click-to-focus users, is this lesson's central mistake — and it's an easy one to make because the form can look completely normal. Visually, unlabeled inputs with nearby placeholder-style text often look identical to properly labeled ones. The difference only shows up when you click the label text and nothing happens, or when a screen reader announces 'edit text, blank' with no idea what it's asking for.

sections.title: Live Example: Change the Input Types
sections.instructions: This is a real, working form. Try clicking each label text (not just the input) — notice it focuses the right field, because they're correctly associated. Then change the type on the 'Email address' input from "text" to "email" and see how the browser's built-in behavior changes (many browsers validate/format email inputs differently from plain text).

sections.label: Predict what will happen if you click the word 'Subscribe to updates' (not the checkbox itself) in the sandbox above — then click it and confirm. Explain why that works, referencing for/id specifically.
sections.hint: This only works because of the label-input association — it wouldn't work if the label and input were unrelated elements that just happened to sit next to each other.

exercises.title: Change 1-2 Inputs, Observe the Result
exercises.brief: In the sandbox above, change the email input's type from "text" to "email", then try typing something without an @ symbol and attempting to submit — note what happens. Then add a third field of your choice (a name field, a password field) with a correctly associated label, and confirm clicking its label focuses it.

quiz.question: A form has a <label>Email</label> sitting visually right next to an <input>, but the label has no 'for' attribute and the input has no matching 'id'. What's the practical consequence?
options: The browser and assistive technology have no actual relationship between them; clicking the label won't focus the input, and a screen reader won't announce what the input is for.
None — visual proximity is all that's needed for them to be associated.
The form will fail to submit entirely.
The input will automatically inherit the label's text as a placeholder.
quiz.explanation: Label-input association is created explicitly through matching for/id attributes, not through visual placement. Without it, a sighted mouse user might not notice anything wrong, but click-to-focus and screen reader announcement — both of which depend on that real association — simply won't work.

quiz.question: Why might a developer not notice a missing label association during their own testing?
options: Because the form will refuse to render at all, making the bug obvious immediately.
Because label association only matters for password fields.
Because all modern browsers auto-fix missing label associations.
Because the visual layout can look completely correct, and the failure only shows up when clicking the label text specifically or using a screen reader.
quiz.explanation: This is a classic 'invisible until you test the right way' accessibility bug — the form looks and mostly behaves normally for a sighted mouse user typing directly into fields, so the missing association only surfaces if you specifically try clicking a label or navigate with a screen reader.

summary: Forms collect input through inputs, labels, and a submit action, and correct label association — a <label>'s for attribute matching its <input>'s id — is what makes a field genuinely usable, not just visually adjacent. That association is what lets clicking label text focus the field and what lets a screen reader announce what an input is actually for; without it, a form can look perfectly normal while quietly failing a real chunk of its users.
interviewQuestions: Why is a label's 'for' attribute necessary if the label already appears right next to its input visually?
How would you test whether a form's labels are actually properly associated with their inputs?

title: Semantic HTML
description: Choosing header/nav/main/article/footer over generic divs to describe what a section of a page actually is.
learningObjectives: Explain and implement: semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, footer) describe the role of a section, improving accessibility and SEO.
Choose the correct semantic element for a given content block, unprompted.
Refactor a div-only layout into semantically meaningful regions.

sections.text: Naming the Regions, Not Just Boxing Them

Semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, footer) describe the role of a section, improving accessibility and SEO. Everything you've learned so far in this module — headings, paragraphs, lists, forms — has been about individual pieces of content. Semantic elements zoom out one level: they say what an entire region of the page is for. A <nav> isn't just a box that happens to hold links; it announces 'this is the navigation' to anyone or anything parsing the page.

sections.text: This is the payoff for everything module-0-2 taught you about DevTools, incidentally. Open the Elements panel on a well-built page and you can read its actual structure at a glance — header, nav, main, article, footer — instead of an undifferentiated forest of <div>s with class names as your only clue. Screen readers expose these same regions as jump targets, letting a user skip straight to 'main content' instead of tabbing through an entire navigation menu first.

Wrapping everything in <div> when a semantic element already exists for that purpose is the mistake this lesson exists to correct — sometimes called 'div soup.' A <div> is not wrong, exactly; it's a legitimate, meaningless container for when nothing more specific fits. The problem is reaching for it out of habit, for a header, a nav menu, or a footer, when an element that actually names that role has existed the whole time.

sections.title: Worked Example: Refactor Div Soup
sections.instructions: This page is built entirely out of <div>s with class names as the only hint of their purpose. Refactor it to use header, nav, main, article, and footer where each one fits — without changing anything about what's visually on screen.

sections.title: Why not just use CSS classes to name everything?
sections.subtitle: Class names are for you; semantic tags are for machines too
sections.content: A class name like class="page-header" communicates intent to another human reading your code — but it means nothing to a browser, a screen reader, or a search engine. Semantic tags carry that meaning at the platform level: assistive technology has built-in support for jumping between <nav>, <main>, and other landmarks, and search engines weight content inside <article> and <main> differently than an anonymous <div>. Classes and semantic tags aren't competing solutions — you'll use both together, a semantic tag for the role, classes for styling hooks.

sections.label: Without a reference, name which semantic element you'd use for: a page's site-wide top banner, a block of unrelated sidebar content, a single self-contained blog post that could stand alone, and the primary content area of a page.
sections.hint: One of these four doesn't have an obvious answer from this lesson alone — that's intentional; make your best reasoned guess and check it against the resources below.

exercises.title: Refactor a Real Page's Div Soup
exercises.brief: Find a simple page you've built in an earlier module exercise (or write a short one now: a header, a nav, one article, a footer). Mark it up first using only <div>s with class names, then refactor it into the correct semantic elements. Write one sentence on what changed for a screen reader user, even though nothing changed visually.

quiz.question: What is the main practical advantage of <nav> over <div class="nav">, given that both can be styled identically?
options: <nav> is understood by assistive technology and search engines as a navigation landmark, regardless of what class names are or aren't present.
<nav> renders faster than a div in every browser.
There is no real difference — they're purely stylistic synonyms.
<nav> automatically generates a website's menu items.
quiz.explanation: A class name is metadata for humans reading the code and for CSS selectors — it carries no meaning to a screen reader or search engine on its own. <nav> is understood at the platform level as a navigation landmark, which is what lets assistive tech offer 'skip to navigation' regardless of what, if anything, the developer named it with CSS classes.

quiz.question: Is using <div> ever the correct choice, even when other semantic elements exist?
options: No — <div> should never appear in well-written HTML.
Yes, but only inside a <table>.
No — <div> is deprecated in modern HTML.
Yes — <div> is a legitimate, meaningless container for grouping content when no more specific semantic element actually fits; the mistake is reaching for it out of habit when one does.
quiz.explanation: <div> isn't the villain here — it's a genuinely useful, intentionally meaningless container for cases where no semantic element fits the content's role. The mistake this lesson targets is defaulting to <div> for a header, nav, or footer specifically, when an element naming that exact role has been available the entire time.

summary: Semantic elements — header, nav, main, article, footer, and others — name what a region of a page actually is, not just how it should be boxed and styled. That meaning is understood by assistive technology and search engines at the platform level, in a way CSS class names never are. <div> remains legitimate for genuinely generic grouping; the mistake is reaching for it out of habit when a semantic element already names the role you need.
interviewQuestions: What's the practical difference between <div class="header"> and <header>?
How would you explain to a teammate why 'div soup' is worth refactoring, given that it looks identical to users?
Name three semantic HTML5 elements and the role each one communicates.

title: HTML Challenge: Build a Real Page

sections.text: Everything This Module Taught, in One Page

Capstone: assemble headings, text, links, images, lists, forms, and semantic structure into one real page. There's no new theory in this lesson — every concept you need was covered in the seven lessons before this one. What's being tested now is whether you can compose them together into something that actually holds up as a real page, not just as seven isolated exercises.

Build the semantic skeleton first — header, nav, main, footer — empty if you have to, before filling in content. Composing a page region-by-region, the way you practiced in the Semantic HTML lesson, produces a much more solid result than writing everything as one long flat sequence of tags and trying to organize it afterward.

sections.text: Building the page as one big flat block instead of composing it from the semantic regions just learned is the trap here — it's tempting to just start typing content top to bottom and worry about structure later, but that's exactly backwards from the habit this module has been building. If you build flat and try to retrofit <header>/<main>/<footer> onto it afterward, you'll almost always end up with regions that don't cleanly contain what they should.

quiz.question: Why does this capstone lesson deliberately avoid introducing any new HTML concepts?
options: Because capstones are meant to be easier than the lessons before them.
Because HTML has no more concepts left to teach after this module.
Because grading is easier when no new material is involved.
Because the goal is testing whether previously taught concepts can be composed together into one coherent, real page — not testing new knowledge.
quiz.explanation: A capstone's purpose is synthesis, not new theory — it tests whether the individually-practiced pieces (headings, links, images, lists, forms, semantic regions) can actually be composed into one working, coherent artifact, which is a meaningfully different and harder skill than executing each piece in isolation.

quiz.question: What's the recommended order of operations for building a page like this capstone, based on this module?
options: Build the semantic skeleton (header/main/footer) first, then fill each region in with content.
Write all the content first, in any order, then retrofit semantic tags around it afterward.
Start with the form, since it's the most complex element.
Order doesn't matter as long as the final HTML validates.
quiz.explanation: Building the semantic regions first, then composing content into them, tends to produce a cleaner result than writing everything flat and reorganizing afterward — retrofitting semantic structure onto already-written flat content is exactly the failure mode this lesson's mistake callout warns about.

summary: The capstone combines everything this module taught — headings, text, links, images, lists, forms, and semantic structure — into one real page, with no new theory introduced.
